strengths: Soundness: The paper gives a substantial, largely self-contained theoretical treatment, including explicit algorithms, assumptions, confidence bonuses, a belief-estimation construction with label alignment, and detailed proofs. The staging argument addresses a genuine dependence obstacle in the state-dependent reward model.

Significance: Obtaining a high-probability sublinear regret bound of order O~(T^{7/8}) when rewards jointly depend on latent states, contexts, and actions—and states may switch frequently—is potentially useful. The O~(T^{3/4}) analysis of the simpler belief-dependent model also improves the type of guarantee previously reported.

Originality: The direct state-dependent formulation is meaningfully more general than reducing rewards to linear functions of beliefs. The combination of staged parameter updates, HMM forgetting, and online belief estimation provides useful new understanding even though several ingredients come from prior work.

Presentation and ethics: The main model, source of the dependence problem, and proof strategy are generally explained clearly. The work is foundational theory with no evident material ethical concern, and its limitations section candidly identifies the lack of optimality results and the poor failure-probability dependence.
weaknesses: Soundness/implementability: The main algorithm is advertised with all HMM parameters unknown, but its confidence bonus in Theorem 5.2 explicitly requires the forgetting coefficient γ. It also uses Cη and Cθ*, none of which are declared known inputs or supplied with computable upper bounds. Since these quantities affect arm selection through action-dependent confidence widths, this is not merely an analysis constant; the stated strategy is not implementable under its declared information model.

Evaluation and reproducibility: There are no numerical results, code, or executable implementation. Appendix F consists only of the sentence that simulations will be supplied in a future version. This leaves computational feasibility, numerical stability of repeated spectral estimation and label alignment, and practical behavior of the very long stages entirely untested.

Significance is limited by the benchmark: Regret is measured against an oracle using b_t=P(h_t|x_1:t), deliberately excluding reward history even though rewards are informative about the latent state. Consequently, the benchmark is weaker than a policy using all observations, pseudo-regret can fail to characterize decision quality against the natural information-state oracle, and the paper does not quantify the gap between these benchmarks. Remark 2.4 does not resolve this issue.

The concrete HMM guarantee is highly restrictive: it assumes a known number of states, finite observation alphabet, stationary initialization, full-rank emissions, invertible transition matrix, and strictly positive entries in both emissions and transitions. The resulting unknown burn-in T_{B,M,ν} can be enormous because it depends exponentially on ill-conditioning constants. The continuous-context extension is mentioned but not instantiated with a complete end-to-end theorem.

Originality is somewhat overstated: the manuscript itself attributes the key L2/Markov covariance argument to Nelson et al.; spectral HMM estimation, filtering-error transfer, and LinUCB machinery are also existing components. The main novelty is therefore their careful combination and extension, rather than an entirely new estimation or concentration method.

Presentation needs another revision: the first contribution paragraph ends mid-sentence (“balance”), Theorem 5.2 incorrectly calls Assumption 2.3 sub-Gaussian although it only assumes a bounded conditional second moment, and the empty future-work simulation appendix makes the submitted version visibly incomplete. These issues complicate verification of an already lengthy 43-page argument.

strengths: Originality/significance: The paper identifies a meaningful distinction between rewards depending on posterior beliefs and rewards depending directly on latent states. The latter is a more natural and technically harder model, and obtaining sublinear regret under linearly frequent state changes would be useful.

Soundness: The staged construction and filtration argument are technically interesting. The manuscript provides extensive proofs, explicit confidence bonuses, and a plausible route to a high-probability O-tilde(T^{7/8}) pseudo-regret bound.
Presentation: The main conceptual obstacle—past rewards make actions informative about latent states—is explained clearly, and the comparison with the belief-dependent model helps motivate staging.
Reproducibility: Most assumptions, algorithms, constants, and proof steps are stated explicitly, including a concrete spectral HMM-estimation subroutine and an alignment procedure.
Ethics: This is foundational bandit theory with no evident material ethical risk; the generic impact statement is adequate for the scope of the work.
weaknesses: Soundness/implementability: The headline claim of a fully adaptive strategy is not supported as stated. The confidence bonus in Theorem 5.2 requires the HMM forgetting coefficient gamma as well as C_eta and C_theta, although the HMM and reward parameters are declared unknown and no known bounds, estimation procedure, or adaptive tuning method is provided. Thus the analyzed algorithm cannot generally be run with the stated information.

Soundness: Lemma 4.3 does not establish Assumption 4.1 as written. The alignment proof only shows that estimated state h converges to true state bar-rho(h) for an unknown permutation bar-rho, whereas Assumption 4.1 requires ||b_hat_t-b_t||_1 to be small in the original coordinates. The claim that ordering is irrelevant to this norm is false unless the true beliefs and reward parameters are simultaneously relabeled. Such a without-loss-of-generality relabeling may repair the argument, but it must be made explicitly and propagated through the theorem.

Algorithmic completeness: The concrete spectral procedure is defined only from t>=3 and can return negative or non-normalized transition/emission estimates. The manuscript mentions clipping and normalization only as something to be done in future numerical experiments; it does not define a valid probability-valued belief subroutine at every round or analyze the effect of this post-processing.

Evidence/significance: There is no empirical evaluation whatsoever. Appendix F consists only of the sentence that simulations will appear in a future version. Consequently, claims of efficiency and practical usefulness are unsupported, and there is no evidence showing when the proposed method improves over prior approaches or how severe the T^{7/8} behavior and very large burn-in constants are.

Evaluation scope: The principal guarantee concerns a context-only pseudo-regret benchmark that deliberately ignores information about the state contained in observed rewards. Since the learner's actions do depend on those rewards, this quantity is not a standard conditional regret and can even have negative instantaneous terms. The manuscript merely asserts, without a formal theorem, that realized cumulative reward can be handled similarly.

Limitations: The discussion focuses almost exclusively on improving regret exponents. It does not adequately address reliance on strong full-rank, strictly positive, stationary finite-observation HMM assumptions; knowledge of the number of states and mixing constants; computational cost of repeatedly running spectral estimation and permutation alignment; or the weakness of the benchmark.

Presentation/reliability: Numerous inconsistencies reduce confidence in a delicate proof: Theorem 5.2 calls Assumption 2.3 “sub-Gaussian” although it only assumes a bounded second moment; the text alternates between eigenvalues and singular values for a nonsymmetric transition matrix; several indices and variables are mistyped; and the paper refers to nonexistent numerical experiments. These are especially problematic in a submission whose contribution is almost entirely theoretical.

Reproducibility: No code is supplied, the proposed post-processing and early-round behavior are unspecified, and the unknown constants needed by the confidence bonuses preclude reproducing the claimed algorithm directly. The detailed appendix is valuable but does not overcome these missing operational details.

strengths: Soundness: The paper provides a substantial, largely self-contained theoretical analysis. Its central result gives a high-probability pseudo-regret bound of order T^{7/8} for rewards depending jointly on latent state, context, and action, under explicit boundedness, belief-estimation, and HMM-forgetting assumptions. The staged construction addresses a genuine dependence problem that prevents a direct LinUCB reduction.

Originality: The distinction between belief-dependent rewards and genuinely state-dependent rewards is important and clearly explained. The staged filtration and associated covariance analysis offer a useful treatment of the harder state-dependent setting, while the T^{3/4} analysis also strengthens the treatment of the simpler Nelson et al. model by incorporating online belief-estimation error.

Presentation: The main technical challenge, algorithm, and proof architecture are communicated clearly. Detailed appendices cover the confidence bounds, spectral HMM estimation, label alignment, forgetting conditions, and staged elliptical-potential argument, making the theoretical results reasonably auditable.

Significance: This establishes a nontrivial sublinear guarantee in a setting allowing continuously valued, context-dependent rewards and latent states that may change at a linear rate, going beyond prior results that omit one of these features or assume infrequent switching.

Limitations and ethics: The paper openly identifies uncertainty about optimal rates and the weakness introduced by the L2-Markov argument. The generic impact statement is adequate for this low-risk theoretical contribution, and no material ethical concern is apparent.
weaknesses: Soundness and implementability: The advertised fully adaptive algorithm is not presently implementable as stated without additional knowledge. The confidence bonus in Theorem 5.2 depends on C_theta, C_eta, and especially the HMM forgetting coefficient gamma, although the algorithm declares the reward and HMM parameters unknown and the assumptions only assert that these constants exist. The authors should either assume known valid bounds explicitly or provide an adaptive tuning/doubling argument.

Evaluation and reproducibility: There are no experiments; Appendix F merely says simulations will appear in a later version. Although experiments are not indispensable for a theorem paper, the absence of any numerical validation leaves the practical behavior of the very conservative T^{3/4}-length stages, spectral estimator, alignment procedure, and large confidence bonuses unknown. No implementation or code is supplied, and the manuscript itself mentions unanalysed clipping and normalization in a prospective implementation.

Significance: The guarantee is for a context-only-belief pseudo-regret benchmark b_t=P(h_t|x_{1:t}), even though the learner observes rewards that contain information about the latent state. This benchmark is weaker than the optimal history-dependent policy using all observations and can even be outperformed by a reward-informed learner. The paper should more sharply delimit what its result says about decision quality in the underlying partially observed problem.

Assumptions and reach: The concrete belief-estimation result requires a known number of states, stationary initialization, finite observations, full-column-rank strictly positive emissions, and an invertible strictly positive transition matrix; the main theorem additionally requires strong uniform exponential forgetting. These conditions substantially narrow the claimed generality, while the continuous-context extension is only referenced rather than instantiated in the theorem.

Optimality and evidence: The T^{7/8} rate is close to linear, no lower bound establishes that staging or a polynomial loss is necessary, and there is no empirical or theoretical comparison showing when the method improves over simpler baselines. The novelty is therefore meaningful but presently more technical than definitive.

Presentation contains several correctable technical inconsistencies, including calling Assumption 2.3 “sub-Gaussian” in Theorem 5.2 even though it only assumes bounded conditional second moments, describing sigma_min(M) as an eigenvalue rather than a singular value for a generally nonsymmetric matrix, and referring to future numerical experiments despite providing none.
